docs.title: zeek-beacon-floor
docs.text:
Beacon hunting guidance says to capture at least

12 hours of traffic,

24 ideally.

No detector sees a clock. What they consume is inter arrival times, and how many of those a capture window yields depends entirely on the beacon's period, which is the one thing a hunter does not know before they look.

This measures the detection floor in the units detectors actually work in, intervals observed and jitter, and converts it back into hours so the guidance becomes checkable.

docs.title: Read this first
docs.text:
Every number here is a simulation. No conn.log from a real network was used. One behaviour is sourced, Cobalt Strike's jitter semantics; everything else is a declared choice.

  • Sources separates what was sourced from what was chosen.
  • Limitations leads with something more important than the simulation: this measures periodic against not periodic, and nothing here separates malicious from benign.

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
interval-cv needs

32 intervals at full jitter. That single floor converts into

0.5 hours of capture for a one minute beacon and

768 hours for a daily one, which is a month.

The plain dispersion statistic beats both spectral detectors, and bowley-skew finds a beacon only when it has no jitter at all, which is the blindness it declares. Both results are on the results page.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install zeek-beacon-floor

zbf fields conn.log         # what this Zeek version called things
zbf score conn.log          # rank the pairs
zbf hours --periods 3600    # how long must I watch for an hourly beacon?
zbf detectors               # what each one ranks by, and is blind to

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• ADR 001: measure in intervals observed, not hours of capture.
  • ADR 002: when in doubt, be generous to the detectors, and say so.
  • ADR 003: keep the detector that fails.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Read this before quoting any number from this project.

docs.title: It is a simulation, end to end
docs.text:
No conn.log from a real network was used. The beacons are generated and so is the background traffic, because no real capture was available to the environment this was built in.

What the project can legitimately claim: under a stated set of assumptions, these detectors need this many observed intervals, and the conversion from intervals to hours of capture spans orders of magnitude depending on the beacon period. The first half is a statement about the detectors. The second half is arithmetic, and holds regardless of how realistic the traffic was.

What it cannot claim: that a hunter running these detectors on a real network would see these numbers.

docs.title: It measures periodic against not periodic, which is not the question
docs.text:
This is the most important line on the page.

A monitoring agent checking in every sixty seconds is periodic. So is a software update check, a certificate revocation poll, an NTP client and a heartbeat to a load balancer. Every detector here scores them exactly as it scores a beacon, because they are beacons in every respect except intent.

No timing statistic separates malicious from benign. The separation measured here is periodic from non periodic, and a deployment turns that into alerts by adding things this tool does not have: knowledge of what the destination is, whether the software is expected on that host, what the payload sizes look like, and whether anyone can account for it.

The false positive rate in these results is therefore not a prediction of a hunter's alert volume. It is computed against non periodic traffic only, for the reasons in ADR 002, and a real network's periodic benign traffic sits entirely above it.

docs.title: Every number is a lower bound on the difficulty
docs.text:
Two assumptions are generous to the detectors, both deliberate:

  • Thresholds are recalibrated at every point in the sweep. A deployment runs one fixed threshold and does worse.
  • Beacons are generated with a single stable period. A beacon whose operator changes the sleep mid capture defeats the spectral detectors entirely and degrades the dispersion ones.

docs.title: The background traffic is two distributions, not a network
docs.text:
Half memoryless, half session traffic. Real network traffic is neither, and in particular it contains:

  • Periodic benign traffic, excluded here for the reasons above.
  • Traffic whose rate changes with the working day, so a window that spans a lunch break has structure that neither model produces.
  • Retries and failures, which cluster connections in ways that look regular at short timescales.

The second and third both push toward more false positives than reported.

docs.title: The jitter models are uniform, and real jitter may not be
docs.text: Both models draw uniformly, one sided for cobalt-strike and two sided for symmetric. A framework that jitters on a different distribution, or that jitters in a pattern rather than independently per check in, is not covered. This matters most for bowley-skew, which is a shape test: it fails here because uniform jitter is nearly skew free, and a genuinely skewed jitter distribution is the one case where it might work.

docs.title: The detectors are the obvious five
docs.text:
Dispersion, dispersion robust to outliers, shape, autocorrelation, spectrum. Not here: anything using payload sizes, which is the strongest signal a real hunter has after timing; anything using the destination's reputation or category; anything learning a per host baseline over weeks; anything correlating several pairs from the same host.

A tool with those would have a different and lower floor, which is a reason to read these numbers as a floor for timing alone rather than for beacon detection in general.

docs.title: The floor is read off a grid
docs.text: Intervals are sampled at 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96 and 128, so a floor reported as 24 means "24 was the first grid point to reach the target" and the true value is somewhere above 16. The grid is coarse at the top on purpose, because that is the region where the answer is "more than you are going to get".

docs.title: These results have been reviewed from the outside exactly once
docs.text:
That review found four defects, and two of them had changed published numbers: a guard that tested exact floating point equality, so a perfect beacon was scored from rounding noise; and a mismatch where the generated beacons carried one more interval than the background traffic they were calibrated against, so the false positive rate was a rate at a different series length than the detection rate beside it.

Neither was findable by rerunning the benchmark, adding seeds, or reading the results, because the output was self consistent and there was a true statement available that explained it. Both were found by a reader given the code and no expectations.

The honest reading is that the numbers here have survived one outside read. That is more than most published benchmarks and much less than enough.

docs.title: What would make this stronger
docs.text:
In roughly descending order of how much it would change the conclusions:

  1. Run it against one real conn.log with a known beacon in it.
  2. Add benign periodic traffic as a third class and report the three way confusion, rather than excluding it.
  3. Add a payload size signal and measure how much of the floor it removes.
  4. Model a beacon whose period changes mid capture.
  5. More seeds and a finer grid.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Generated by tools/generate_results_doc.py from docs/metrics.json. Reproduce with make bench.

docs.title: Every figure here is a simulation
docs.text: Every figure in this file is a simulation. The beacons are generated and so is the background traffic; no conn.log from a real network was used. Jitter semantics are sourced from Cobalt Strike's sleep command, where the jitter percentage only shortens the sleep. Everything else, including the composition of the background traffic, is a declared choice.

docs.title: The floor, in intervals observed
docs.text:
The fewest observed intervals at which a detector finds 90% of beacons, at a 1% false positive rate against non periodic traffic. Averaged over 8 seeds of 300 samples per class, under the cobalt-strike jitter model.

never means the target was not reached at any point in the grid, which tops out at 128 intervals.

detector jitter 0.0 jitter 0.2 jitter 0.4 jitter 0.6 jitter 0.8 jitter 1.0 interval-cv 4 4 4 6 12 32 mad-ratio 4 4 8 16 32 never bowley-skew 4 never never never never never autocorrelation 6 12 48 never never never spectral 8 16 96 never never never

Reaching the target at every jitter in the grid: interval-cv. The dispersion statistics hold up better than the spectral ones, which is the opposite of what the extra machinery in a spectral method suggests.

docs.title: What each detector cannot see
docs.text:
detector needs at least blind to interval-cv 3 intervals a single missed check in, which the standard deviation turns into irregularity, and two interleaved beacons, which look like one irregular one mad-ratio 3 intervals a slow drift in the interval, which stays close to the median throughout; anything about the order the intervals arrived in; and a bare majority of identical intervals, which sets the deviation to zero and scores a perfect 1 however wild the rest are bowley-skew 4 intervals symmetric jitter of any size, which is skew free and therefore scores like a perfect beacon, so this is a shape test and not a regularity test autocorrelation 6 intervals a beacon whose interval changes during the capture, which has no single lag, and anything shorter than sixteen bins spectral 6 intervals the same drift autocorrelation misses, and a beacon running at a period close to the capture length, which has too few cycles to form a peak

Each of these was written before the sweep ran. bowley-skew declared that symmetric jitter is skew free and therefore indistinguishable from no jitter, and the measurement then found it detecting almost nothing.

docs.title: The same floor, in hours of capture
docs.text:
Guidance for beacon hunting recommends capturing at least 12 hours, with 24 being more ideal. A detector does not see a clock, so the same floor converts into very different capture windows depending on the beacon's period.

Hours of capture needed by interval-cv, the strongest detector here:

beacon period jitter 0.0 jitter 0.2 jitter 0.4 jitter 0.6 jitter 0.8 jitter 1.0 1 minute 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.2 0.5 5 minutes 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.5 1.0 2.7 1 hour 4.0 4.0 4.0 6.0 12.0 32.0 1 day 96.0 96.0 96.0 144.0 288.0 768.0

A one minute beacon is found inside 0.5 hours even at the worst jitter in the grid, so the 12 hour advice is generous for it. A daily beacon needs 768 hours at that jitter and 96 hours with no jitter at all, which is weeks rather than a day. The guidance is not wrong; the unit hides a dependency on the thing the hunter does not know.

docs.title: The jitter model is not a detail
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike's jitter only shortens the sleep: sleep 300 20 produces 240 to 300 seconds. The symmetric model most tooling assumes varies the interval both ways, spreading it over twice the range at the same stated percentage. These are different experiments.

detector jitter cobalt-strike symmetric interval-cv 0.0 4 4 interval-cv 0.2 4 4 interval-cv 0.4 4 6 interval-cv 0.6 6 8 interval-cv 0.8 12 16 interval-cv 1.0 32 32 mad-ratio 0.0 4 4 mad-ratio 0.2 4 6 mad-ratio 0.4 8 12 mad-ratio 0.6 16 24 mad-ratio 0.8 32 64

A floor quoted at a jitter percentage means two different things depending on which model was meant, which is worth knowing before comparing any two beacon detection results.

docs.title: Missed check ins
docs.text:
A real beacon misses: a laptop closes, a link drops. With 20% of check ins removed, the intervals a detector sees include gaps of two and three periods.

detector jitter 0.4, no misses jitter 0.4, with misses interval-cv 4 16 mad-ratio 8 16 bowley-skew never never autocorrelation 48 96 spectral 96 never

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text:
pairs connections all five detectors 1,000 25,000 0.59s 10,000 250,000 6.66s

250,000 connections scored by every detector in 6.7 seconds, which is a conn.log sized problem on a laptop.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: What this project took from outside itself, and what it made up. Every figure published here is a simulation, so the distinction matters more than usual.

docs.title: The sourced behaviour the project turns on
docs.text:
Cobalt Strike, sleep command. https://hstechdocs.helpsystems.com/manuals/cobaltstrike/current/userguide/content/topics/post-exploitation_asynch-interactive.htm

sleep takes a time in seconds and an optional jitter percentage. The documentation states that Beacon varies each check in time by that percentage, and that sleep 300 20 produces a random sleep between 240 and 300 seconds. Jitter only ever shortens the sleep: the configured interval is a maximum.

This is the cobalt-strike jitter model in zbf.synth, and it is the model the headline floor is measured under. It matters because the symmetric model, where the interval varies both ways around the nominal value, spreads intervals over twice the range at the same stated percentage. A floor quoted at "30 percent jitter" means two different things depending on which was meant, and the benchmark reports both rather than picking one.

Other C2 frameworks implement jitter differently, and the default here follows the one with documented semantics rather than assuming it generalises.

docs.title: The guidance this project is measured against
docs.text:
Active Countermeasures, beacon analysis guidance. https://www.activecountermeasures.com/threat-hunting-simplifying-the-beacon-analysis-process/

Recommends capturing at least twelve hours of traffic, with twenty four hours being more ideal, so that multiple beacon instances are recorded, and describes beacon scores on a zero to one scale.

Those two numbers are the red lines on the right hand panel of the floor chart. The guidance is not wrong; it is stated in a unit that hides a dependency on the beacon period, which is what ADR 001 is about.

docs.title: The log format
docs.text:
Zeek, conn.log. https://docs.zeek.org/en/lts/logs/conn.html

Field names and the two on disk formats, tab separated with a #fields header and JSON lines. The relevant detail for this project is that the field set is not stable across versions: Zeek 8 added ip_proto, which shifts the position of every column after it. That is why zbf.conn reads names from the header and refuses a headerless TSV rather than assuming positions, and why a test asserts a Zeek 7 record and a Zeek 8 record parse identically.

docs.title: Everything else is a declared choice
docs.text:
The following are not sourced from anywhere. They are stated in the benchmark's conditions block and in docs/metrics.json so a reader can disagree with them specifically:

  • The composition of the background traffic: half memoryless, half session traffic in bursts. Real networks are neither.
  • The false positive rate the thresholds are set at, one percent.
  • The detection rate the floor is defined at, ninety percent.
  • The beacon periods drawn per sample, uniform between thirty seconds and an hour. Every detector here is scale free and a test asserts it, so this should not affect any result, and drawing it is how that claim is tested rather than assumed.
  • The share of missed check ins in experiment C.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Bowley skewness. A quartile based measure of asymmetry, (Q3 + Q1 - 2 * Q2) / (Q3 - Q1), chosen over the third moment because it is defined on small samples without the variance of a cubed term. It is the basis of the bowley-skew detector. It appeared not to work at all until an outside review found that the guard for a degenerate spread tested exact floating point equality, so a perfect beacon was scored from rounding noise. See ADR 003.

Autocorrelation through the frequency domain. The arrival train is binned, transformed, multiplied by its own conjugate and transformed back, which is the Wiener Khinchin route to the same answer np.correlate gives by direct convolution, at O(n log n) instead of O(n squared).

docs.title: ADR 001: measure the floor in intervals observed, not hours of capture
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Beacon hunting guidance is stated in hours. Active Countermeasures recommends capturing at least twelve hours of traffic, with twenty four being more ideal, so that multiple beacon instances are recorded. That advice is widely repeated and it is the operational knob a hunter actually turns.

No detector in this project, and none in any beacon analysis tool, can see a clock. What every one of them consumes is a sequence of inter arrival times. How many of those a capture window yields depends entirely on the beacon's period, which is the one thing a hunter does not know before they look.

A twelve hour capture yields 720 intervals from a sixty second beacon and twelve from an hourly one. Those are not the same measurement, and no amount of care about the capture window changes that.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Measure and publish the floor in intervals observed and jitter, which are the units the detectors operate in, and provide the conversion to hours as a derived table rather than as the primary result.

zbf hours performs the conversion, taking the floor in intervals and a beacon period and returning the capture window a hunter has to plan for. That command is the point of the project; zbf floor is the measurement behind it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The headline result is a grid over intervals and jitter, which is less immediately actionable than a number of hours and is the honest shape of the answer.
  • The conversion makes the guidance checkable instead of contradicting it. For a fast beacon the twelve hour advice is generous. For a slow one it is short by more than an order of magnitude, and the table says by how much.
  • A hunter using this has to assume a beacon period to get an answer in hours, which is uncomfortable and correct: they were always assuming one, and the conversion makes the assumption visible rather than removing it.
  • Everything scale free in the codebase stays that way, and a test asserts it: the same series scaled from thirty seconds to a day must score identically under every detector. Without that property the conversion would not be sound.

docs.title: What this does not claim
docs.text: That the twelve hour guidance is wrong. It is advice about a capture window given without knowledge of the beacon period, which is the only advice anyone can give in that unit. The claim is narrower: the unit hides a dependency, the dependency spans orders of magnitude, and a hunter who knows the period they are hunting can do better than a fixed window.

docs.title: ADR 002: when in doubt, be generous to the detectors
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A floor measurement has several free choices, and most of them can be set to make detection look easy or hard. A project whose conclusion is that detection is harder than the guidance implies has an obvious incentive to set them the hard way, and would deserve to be disbelieved for it.

Two choices mattered most.

Where the threshold comes from. A detector's score distribution on background traffic shifts as the series gets longer, so a single threshold calibrated once performs differently at four intervals than at sixty four.

What counts as a negative. Real networks are full of periodic traffic that is not a beacon: monitoring agents, update checks, certificate revocation polls, NTP.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Resolve both in the direction that flatters the detectors, and say so in the output rather than in a footnote.

Thresholds are recalibrated at every point in the sweep, from background traffic with the same number of intervals. A deployed detector runs one fixed threshold and does worse than this.

Negatives are non periodic traffic only. Benign periodic traffic is excluded from the negative class entirely.

docs.title: Why exclude the traffic that causes real false positives
docs.text:
Because including it would measure the wrong thing twice over.

A monitoring agent checking in every sixty seconds is periodic. It scores like a beacon under every detector here, and it should, because it is a beacon in every respect except intent. Counting it as a negative would make the reported false positive rate a measure of how much monitoring software the simulated network happens to run, which is a number about the simulation and not about the detector.

It would also quietly change the question. These detectors separate periodic from non periodic. Nothing in a timing statistic separates malicious from benign, and a false positive rate computed against benign beacons would imply the tool was attempting a separation it cannot make.

So the measurement is of the separation the detectors can do, and the separation they cannot do is stated plainly in the README and in docs/limitations.md rather than buried in a metric.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every floor in this repository is a lower bound on the difficulty. A deployment does worse, for reasons that are named.
  • The reported false positive rate is not a prediction of a hunter's alert volume, and the documentation does not let it be read as one.
  • zbf score prints, under every result, that a high score means periodic and not malicious. A test asserts that sentence is still there, because it is the one line in the tool most likely to be lost to an edit.

docs.title: ADR 003: the detector that failed, and why the explanation was wrong
docs.text: Status: accepted, after being rewritten Date: 2026-10-21

docs.title: What this decision was originally
docs.text:
bowley-skew scores beacons by one minus the absolute Bowley skewness of their intervals. In the first sweep it reached the target detection rate nowhere: not at any number of intervals, not at any jitter, including no jitter at all.

The decision was to keep it anyway and publish the row of failures, and the argument was this:

The failure was predicted and then observed. blind_to was written from the mathematics before the sweep ran, and the sweep found what it said. That is the strongest available evidence that the declaration requirement is doing real work rather than generating plausible prose.

That argument was wrong, and the way it was wrong is worth more than the decision it was defending.

docs.title: What was actually happening
docs.text:
Bowley skewness is (Q3 + Q1 - 2*Q2) / (Q3 - Q1). The denominator is zero when every interval in the middle half is identical, which is what a perfect beacon looks like, so the code guarded it:

if spread <= 0:
    return 1.0

That guard catches only exact floating point equality. A perfect beacon's intervals are not exactly equal. They are produced by np.diff(np.cumsum(sleeps)), and the running sum accumulates rounding error whenever the period is not representable in binary, which is almost always. A perfect beacon with a period of 2047.3771254706232 seconds has an interquartile spread of 4.5e-13 seconds, which is not zero, so the skewness was computed as a ratio of two quantities that were both pure rounding noise.

The result was a scale free statistic applied to numerical dust. A perfect beacon scored 0.0. Across periods drawn the way the benchmark draws them, 39 percent of perfect beacons scored below 0.5 and only 45 percent scored 1.0. The one percent false positive threshold for this detector sits near 0.99, so most perfect beacons were misses before any jitter was applied at all.

The fix is a relative guard rather than an exact one: treat a spread that is negligible against the median as degenerate. After it, every one of 4000 perfect beacons scores 1.0, and the detector reaches the target at low jitter.

docs.title: Why the wrong explanation survived
docs.text:
The declared blindness was real. Uniform jitter is nearly skew free in both models, so bowley-skew genuinely does struggle as jitter rises, and it genuinely is a shape test rather than a regularity test.

So when the sweep produced a row of failures, there was a true statement available that explained it, and the explanation was flattering: a declaration written before the measurement had predicted the result. It made the blind_to requirement look like it was doing real work. Nothing about the output contradicted it.

What it could not explain, and what nobody asked, is why the detector failed at zero jitter, where its declared blindness does not apply at all. That column was right there in the published table, reading never, and the story had no room for it.

An independent review of the source found the guard. It was not found by rerunning the benchmark, by adding seeds, or by reading the results, because all of those were consistent with the wrong explanation.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Keep bowley-skew, on an argument that no longer depends on the failure:

  • It is a different kind of statistic from the other four, a shape test rather than a dispersion or spectral one, and the comparison is more informative with it than without it.
  • Its real blindness, that uniform jitter is nearly skew free, is a measured result now rather than an unfalsifiable one, because it can be seen degrading from a correct score at zero jitter instead of starting at zero.

And record the methodological consequence, which applies to the whole project:

A result that confirms a declaration is not evidence that the declaration was doing work. It is the case where checking is most needed and least likely, because the explanation is already there and it is satisfying. The discipline that caught this was not internal; it was handing the code to a reader who had not been told what to expect.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The published floors changed. Every number in docs/metrics.json and everything generated from it was re-measured after the fix.
  • A test pins a perfect beacon at 1.0 across 300 randomly drawn periods, so this class of bug cannot return quietly.
  • The same review found three other defects of the same shape, where a true statement was standing in front of a bug. They are in the commit history with the same treatment.
  • docs/limitations.md gains the general version: the results here have been reviewed from the outside once, and the things that survive that are not the same as the things that survive rerunning your own benchmark.
